65% of cloud breaches come from misconfigurations.

Not sophisticated attacks. Not zero-days.
Someone checked "public" when they meant "private."

Last quarter we found:
• 4 S3 buckets publicly exposing customer data
• 7 overly permissive IAM roles (admin to interns)
• 11 security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 inbound

The cloud provider gives you infinite flexibility.
It also gives you infinite rope.

Your security tools might be expensive.
But are they checking what your developers actually deploy?

Infrastructure security review → zerosight360.com

87% of organizations experienced an API security incident last year.

258 attacks per organization on average.
$700K average cost per incident.
5,900+ APIs per enterprise.

Yet most companies:
• Don't have a complete API inventory
• Can't detect shadow APIs
• Have no auth standards enforcement
• Rely solely on WAF for protection

Your API count is growing faster than your team can track.

Shadow APIs from abandoned projects.
Partner integrations nobody documented.
Internal tools with admin endpoints exposed.

Every endpoint is an attack surface.
Do you know where yours are?

API security assessment → zerosight360.com

86% of commercial codebases contain open source vulnerabilities.

You chose your framework carefully.
But your framework chose 911 dependencies on average.

What's 8 levels deep in your dependency tree?
→ Components last updated in 2019
→ Maintainers who moved on
→ Known CVEs nobody patched

And supply chain attacks increased 4× since 2020.

npm audit catches direct deps.
What catches level 8?

Your vendors do security reviews.
Who reviews your open source?

Dependency security audit → zerosight360.com

The zero-day window just shrunk to 5 days.

KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) inclusion dropped from 8.5 to 5 days.
Highly exploitable vulnerabilities up 105% year over year.

Translation:
From public disclosure to active exploitation in under a week.

Can your team answer "are we affected?" in hours?

Most can't because:
• Asset inventory is incomplete
• Dependencies aren't tracked
• Vulnerability scanners run weekly

The attackers check Rapid7 too.
They just move faster.

Real-time visibility isn't optional anymore.

Vulnerability response assessment → zerosight360.com

79% of ransomware attacks start with stolen credentials.

Attackers don't break in. They log in.

The anatomy of access:
→ Password from a breach database
→ Or phishing email (54% click rate with AI)
→ Or session token from malware
→ Then lateral movement via RDP
→ Then data exfiltration
→ Then encryption

MFA helps. But MFA fatigue is real.
(3am approve-button attacks work)

Service accounts are worse:
• Created for integrations
• Given admin rights "temporarily"
• Never audited
• Never rotated
• Shared credentials in Slack

Your perimeter isn't the firewall anymore.
It's every identity with access.

Identity security review → zerosight360.com

Last month I found a client's entire customer database in a public S3 bucket.

Not a sophisticated attack.
Not a supply chain compromise.
I just... looked.

The bucket was set to public during "quick testing" two years ago.
It was supposed to be temporary.

They had expensive security tools.
Annual penetration tests.
SOC 2 Type II certification.

But this bucket was created outside the normal deployment process.
A developer needed something fast.
It worked.
They moved on.

Two years and 200,000 customer records later, I found it in 20 minutes.

The gap isn't technology.
It's visibility.

What exists outside your official infrastructure?

-Nish

AI-crafted phishing emails have a 54% click rate.
Human-written ones? 12%.

I tested this with a client last month.

Same company.
Same employee list.
Two campaigns.

The AI email was perfect:
• Correct tone for the industry
• No grammar mistakes
• Referenced real internal projects
• From a domain that looked legitimate

The old tells don't work anymore.
"Check for spelling errors" is dead advice.
"Does it look professional?" — yes, it does.

We're training employees on outdated threats.

The question isn't "does this look suspicious?"
It's "was I expecting this request?"

Security awareness training needs a rewrite.

-Nish

We found 23 critical vulnerabilities in an "approved" npm package.

Client pulled in a popular React component library.
50K+ weekly downloads.
MIT license.
Active maintainer.
All green flags.

I ran a deep dependency audit anyway.
8 levels down in the dependency tree:
• A package last updated in 2019
• With 23 known CVEs
• Including 2 critical RCEs

npm audit catches direct dependencies.
It does not catch level 8.

The component library maintainer didn't even know it was there.
It was a dependency of a dependency of a dependency.

911 average components per codebase.
86% have vulnerabilities.

Who audits your audits?

-Nish

A client called me at 11pm last week.

"We just saw the CVE. Are we affected?"

They weren't sure.
Their asset inventory was a spreadsheet from 6 months ago.
Their dependency list was "whatever's in package.json" (direct deps only).
Their infrastructure had grown 40% since last audit.

We spent 4 hours answering a question that should take 4 minutes.

The zero-day window is now 5 days.
From public disclosure to active exploitation.

You don't have time to figure out what you have when the CVE drops.
You need to know before.

What would happen if a critical CVE dropped in your stack tonight?

Could you answer "are we affected?" before coffee?

-Nish

25.7% of AI-generated code contains security vulnerabilities.

I reviewed a codebase last month.
50% of it was written by Copilot.
The developer was honest about it.

The AI was efficient:
• Clean structure
• Good variable names
• Fast to implement

The AI was also dangerous:
• SQL concatenation instead of parameterized queries
• User input passed directly to shell commands
• JWT tokens stored in localStorage
• CORS set to wildcard

The developer trusted the suggestions.
The suggestions came from training data.
The training data included insecure code.

AI makes you code faster.
It doesn't make you code safer.

Human review is now more important, not less.

-Nish
